Deck overview
Verify a computation with a short proof

Suppose a server applies a hash function a million times and claims that the final output is . Checking every intermediate hash would repeat essentially the entire computation. We want a proof that is short to transmit and much cheaper to verify, even when producing it requires substantial work.

A SNARG is a succinct non-interactive argument. “Non-interactive” means that the prover sends one proof string; “argument” means soundness against PPT provers. The lecture’s succinctness convention requires both short proofs and fast verification. For public statement , witness , and security parameter , it writes these as

The notes use multi-argument O notation to collect the allowed costs. The essential restrictions are polynomial dependence on logarithmic witness/input sizes for proof length, and only linear dependence on the public-input length for verification, in addition to the security-parameter costs. A merely polynomial-time verifier does not automatically meet that stronger requirement.

A SNARK additionally has an argument-of-knowledge guarantee: successful proving permits witness extraction under its definition. Zero knowledge is another separate property. This chapter first builds the succinct verification machinery, then explains which additional guarantees a full system needs.

‹
What does each guarantee promise?

Keep four questions separate when reading a proof-system theorem. A language is the set of statements for which a valid witness exists; means the statement is true.

PropertyQuestion it answers
CompletenessDoes an honest proof of a true statement pass?
SoundnessCan a false statement pass?
KnowledgeCan a witness be extracted from a sufficiently successful prover?
Zero knowledgeCan the verifier’s view be simulated without the witness?

Soundness error bounds acceptance on false statements. Knowledge error is the acceptance threshold above which the extraction guarantee applies. An extractor is an efficient algorithm that can interact with a prover, possibly restoring it to an earlier state to ask a different challenge. It has more access than a spectator reading one proof.

A proof’s soundness holds even against an unlimited prover; an argument restricts the attacker to efficient computation. “Efficient” means polynomial time. The formal PPT and negligible-function definitions from Chapter 1 apply to these computational guarantees.

HW3 1a · Knowledge implies soundness

An interactive proof has soundness error greater than : some prover convinces the verifier of a false statement with probability greater than . Can it have knowledge error less than ? Explain your answer.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Soundness concerns false statements. If the public statement is false, there is no witness satisfying the relation .

  2. Knowledge error is the acceptance threshold above which the proof-of-knowledge guarantee requires an efficient extractor to recover a valid witness from the prover. The extractor may interact with and rewind that prover; it does not simply read the transcript.

  3. The cheating prover in the question succeeds with probability greater than . If , that success would trigger extraction on a false statement. This is impossible because no valid witness exists. Thus the sheet’s claim that such a knowledge error is impossible is true.

What information exists before the proof?

Non-interactive means the prover sends one proof without receiving a fresh verifier challenge. How can that message avoid being fabricated by the same kind of simulator that zero knowledge promises? The answer depends on the public setup available to the algorithms.

ModelAvailable resource
Plain modelOnly the statement and public algorithms; no special setup.
CRS modelA common reference string sampled before proofs begin. Its generation and any secret setup information are part of the theorem.
Random-oracle modelAccess to an ideal random function: each new input receives a uniform answer; a repeated input receives the same answer.

In a CRS theorem, the simulator may generate a simulated setup with extra secret information. In a random-oracle theorem, it may be allowed to program oracle answers consistently. These simulation powers need not be available to an actual cheating prover. In the plain model, that distinction is missing.

NP consists of problems with efficiently checkable witnesses. BPP consists of problems an efficient randomized algorithm can decide with error at most . These names will let us state the limitation of plain-model NIZKs precisely in the next exercise. “Standard model” excludes an ideal random oracle but may still allow a CRS.

HW3 1b · Which setup model?

The sheet asks whether we can construct non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP “in the standard model (without a random oracle)”. Explain why the setup model matters.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. A language is the set of true statements. NP means a true statement has a short witness that can be checked efficiently. BPP means an efficient randomized algorithm decides membership, with error at most on each input. Neither definition says every NP problem is in BPP.

  2. In the plain model, the verifier has only the statement, proof and public algorithm description. There is no trusted common reference string (CRS) and no random oracle. A NIZK simulator produces an accepted-looking proof for a true statement without its witness.

  3. Run that simulator on the input and give its output to the verifier. On true inputs, zero knowledge and completeness imply high acceptance. On false inputs, soundness bounds acceptance, because the simulator is an efficient candidate prover. A standard bounded-time simulation (with a timeout if needed) therefore gives a BPP decision procedure.

  4. Consequently, plain-model NIZKs for all NP languages would imply , which is not expected. This is the intended “likely false” answer. But standard model does not necessarily mean plain model: a CRS is compatible with the standard model, and CRS-based NIZKs for NP exist under suitable assumptions. “No random oracle” alone does not justify an impossibility claim.

The three messages we will remove

To understand how we remove interaction, recall the Schnorr proof of knowledge of with . The public group has prime order , with generator ; all exponents are in .

If the prover could choose before , it could sample and set , passing the equation without knowing . This reverse construction is the honest-verifier simulator. The original timing prevents it from being used as a live cheating strategy.

Fiat–Shamir must replace that timing constraint with a reproducible challenge the prover still cannot freely choose. The next card shows how the random oracle supplies it.

Replace the challenge with a hash

Fiat–Shamir makes the challenge reproducible by a future verifier. First fix the statement and first message; then compute their hash:

The prover sends . The verifier derives itself and runs the original check. In the random-oracle model, each fresh input has an unpredictable uniform answer. The prover can choose , but cannot choose the answer after fixing . It can, however, try several first messages. We will account for those attempts shortly.

Bind the whole public context into the hash: statement, protocol identity, parameters and prior messages. Otherwise the same hash input might accidentally serve different claims or protocols. The short notation suppresses fixed context, not a security requirement.

The transform needs a security argument for the particular protocol and model. It does not turn computational privacy into statistical privacy: the former protects against efficient observers, while the latter also protects against unlimited distinguishing computation.

HW3 2a · Construct the Schnorr proof

In Schnorr’s protocol, generates a group of prime order , the public value is , and the prover knows secret exponent . Use Fiat–Shamir to construct a non-interactive proof. What is ?

Show step-by-step solution

  1. The interactive prover first chooses a fresh uniform and sends . The symbol means exponents are reduced modulo . Fresh prevents different proofs from exposing equations with reused secret randomness.

  2. Replace the verifier’s uniform challenge with . In this model, a random oracle assigns an independent uniform challenge to each new encoded input and remembers the answer for repeats. The verifier can compute the same challenge.

  3. Compute the response and send

    The challenge need not be sent because it can be recomputed. In an implementation, also bind the protocol name and group parameters into an unambiguous hash input; is the sheet’s abbreviated notation.

Write the verifier for the proof of knowledge of such that .

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Parse the proof. Check that the public parameters and are valid elements of the intended prime-order group, and that is a valid scalar in . These checks keep the algebra in the domain the protocol assumes.

  2. Recompute using exactly the prover’s encoding and hash domain. Accept precisely when

    The verifier uses public ; it does not need the secret .

  3. To check completeness, substitute the honest response:

    Adding exponents corresponds to multiplying group elements. This identity explains why every honest proof passes; by itself it does not prove soundness against a cheating prover.

HW3 1d · Hashing does not strengthen privacy

True or false: applying Fiat–Shamir to a Sigma protocol always gives statistical zero knowledge.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. A Sigma protocol has a first message, a random challenge and a response. Its honest-verifier zero-knowledge property may be only computational: efficient observers cannot distinguish a real transcript from a simulated one, but an unlimited observer might.

  2. Fiat–Shamir replaces the verifier’s challenge with a hash of the statement and first message. It changes how the challenge is obtained. It does not remove information that an unlimited observer could already recover from those messages.

  3. The claim is false. Statistical zero knowledge must hold even against unlimited distinguishing computation; computational HVZK is not enough to conclude that stronger property. Any Fiat–Shamir security claim also needs the appropriate random-oracle theorem and protocol assumptions.

A public proof and an interactive recording

A non-interactive proof has a public verification rule. Anyone who has the same statement, proof and public setup can apply it. Passing the proof to another person preserves this check.

An interactive ZK recording has a different meaning. Its simulator can create an indistinguishable transcript without the witness. For Schnorr, choose uniform , then compute . This makes the verification equation hold. In a real execution, must have been sent before an independently chosen challenge; the recording alone cannot establish that ordering happened with a real prover.

This is why “a convincing interaction happened” and “these three values satisfy the equation” are different claims.

For a Fiat–Shamir proof, the simulator’s reverse-generated triple must also satisfy . A random-oracle simulation can program that oracle answer consistently, under the theorem’s rules. An ordinary prover cannot set the oracle’s answer. This extra simulation capability explains why a NIZK simulator does not automatically give everyone a way to forge publicly verified proofs.

HW3 2d · Can a proof be passed on?

A verifier accepts a NIZK for a statement. Can it convince another verifier? Compare this with passing on the recorded conversation from an interactive zero-knowledge proof.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. A publicly verifiable NIZK is a proof string . A second verifier with the same statement and public setup can run the same verification algorithm on that string. Copying the proof does not require knowing its witness.

  2. For an interactive ZK proof, the first verifier’s recorded view includes its challenges and the prover’s responses. Zero knowledge promises that an efficient simulator can generate an indistinguishable view without the witness.

  3. Therefore that recorded view alone does not establish to a third party that a real prover participated: it could have been simulated. The distinction is between a transferable public proof and a simulatable record of an interaction. This argument concerns recordings; it is not a claim that every live relay attack is impossible.

Count challenges before counting attempts

Suppose a cheating prover fixes and then queries . For Schnorr with , exactly one of the challenges satisfies . This follows because nonidentity generates the prime-order group, so distinct exponents give distinct powers.

A uniform hash answer hits that challenge with probability . If the attacker tests candidates, the union bound adds their individual success bounds, giving at most , capped at 1. This remains an upper bound without assuming the success events are independent. A repeated oracle input gives the same challenge, not another random opportunity.

For a one-bit challenge there are only two possibilities. An attainable cheating success of is already too large, even before the attacker searches. The next two exercises separate this small-challenge failure from the general counting argument.

HW3 2c · Bound a restricted guessing attack

A cheating prover chooses a response , then a first message , before asking for . Explain the bound for tested candidate proofs. Assume , where 1 is the group identity.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Acceptance requires . Once are fixed, the right side must match one fixed group element. Because the group has prime order and , the map takes each of the scalars to a different group element. Exactly one challenge can work.

  2. A fresh random-oracle answer is uniform among those challenges, so this attempt succeeds with probability . Repeating the same oracle input returns the stored answer; it is not a fresh random attempt.

  3. The union bound says the chance that any of events occurs is at most the sum of their probabilities. Applying it to the tested candidates gives

    The argument is for this prescribed guessing strategy, not a full proof of knowledge for arbitrary attacks.

  4. Here counts all tested candidates. If an attacker makes oracle queries and then submits one additional, unqueried candidate, the same counting argument gives , capped at 1. Also, when , the witness is already public; the “unknown nonzero exponent” argument does not apply.

HW3 3a · A one-bit hash challenge is insufficient

A Sigma protocol has an efficient cheating strategy on a false statement that is accepted with probability . Show why applying Fiat–Shamir directly fails to give negligible soundness error.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Run the cheating strategy to produce its first message on the false statement . Fix before querying . The random-oracle answer has the same uniform challenge distribution as the interactive verifier’s challenge.

  2. Give this challenge to the cheating strategy and submit the resulting response with . The acceptance probability is still , by the assumed attainable cheating success of the original strategy.

  3. A constant does not shrink as the security parameter grows, so it is not negligible. One efficient attempt already violates the desired soundness guarantee. An upper bound of alone would not prove an attack exists; this question uses error as an attainable value.

Make the entire challenge hard to guess

Run copies of a one-bit-challenge Sigma protocol in parallel: send all first messages, receive all challenges, then send all responses. The verifier accepts only if every copy passes.

Why does this help even against a malicious prover that correlates its messages? Fix its whole first-message vector on a false statement. Special soundness implies that a coordinate cannot answer both 0 and 1: if it could, extraction would produce a witness for a false statement. Thus at most one full challenge vector can pass.

The verifier chooses uniformly among all these vectors. We count acceptable vectors rather than assuming a cheating prover behaves like independent honest copies. Fiat–Shamir must then hash the statement and all first messages to obtain the entire vector.

HW3 3b · Amplify before applying Fiat–Shamir

Starting from the one-bit-challenge Sigma protocol, construct a three-message protocol with negligible soundness error. Then explain how to make it non-interactive.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Let be the security parameter. Send first messages together, receive a vector of independent uniform challenge bits, and send all responses together. Accept only if every copy accepts. These are still three messages, each now a batch.

  2. Fix any first-message vector on a false statement. Special soundness says that two accepted responses to different challenges for the same first message would yield a witness. Since the statement is false, no such witness exists. Thus each coordinate can answer at most one of its two challenges, even if a malicious prover correlated its first messages.

  3. At most one of the equally likely challenge vectors can pass all coordinates, so the soundness error is at most , which is negligible. Honest executions retain completeness; independent honest-verifier simulators reproduce the joint honest transcript distribution. Special soundness for the parallel protocol follows by extracting from any coordinate whose challenge differs.

  4. For Fiat–Shamir, derive the whole challenge vector at once:

    Hash only after fixing every first message. Return those messages and their responses. Under the appropriate random-oracle security argument, polynomially many attempts cannot overcome an exponentially large challenge space.

Two routes to a succinct proof

Hashing a challenge can remove interaction, but it does not shorten the information that the verifier needs. For succinctness, we first design a proof in an ideal model where the verifier can query a fixed encoded object without receiving all of it. An interactive oracle proof (IOP) allows such objects to be supplied in rounds.

Oracle interfaceWhat one query returns
PCPA bit at a specified position of a fixed encoded proof.
Linear IOPThe inner product of a supplied weight vector with the fixed proof vector.
Polynomial IOPThe value of a fixed, degree-bounded polynomial at a supplied point.

The prover chooses the object, but cannot invent new answers after learning the query. Soundness in this ideal model can therefore be information-theoretic. Cryptography is used later to enforce the same consistency against an efficient prover.

For a linear query with weights and proof vector , the answer is . Thus polynomial evaluation is a particular linear query to the coefficient vector. This connects the interfaces without identifying their different degree or query restrictions.

Why a few proof bits can be enough

A probabilistically checkable proof (PCP) encodes a witness into a longer proof string , designed so that a small number of local checks can detect a false claim. The PCP theorem does not say that a few random bits of an ordinary witness are enough.

The version supplied for HW3 has proof length , where , and a randomized verifier that reads a constant number of proof positions. Its guarantees are

The superscript means query access to the fixed string . The probability is over verifier randomness. On a false statement, the bound holds for every fixed proof, including one chosen by an unbounded prover.

HW3 assumes nonadaptive queries: their positions are selected from and verifier randomness before the answers are seen. The verifier then applies a specified local predicate to those bits. The lecture highlights constant-query PCPs, including its three-query illustration; the homework construction works with its stated constant .

The remaining challenge is to prevent a real prover from choosing its answers after seeing those positions. A short vector commitment will replace the ideal fixed-proof interface.

Commit to the proof before revealing queries

A vector commitment binds a public commitment to an indexed list of values. For a Merkle tree, hash the proof bits as ordered leaves, hash ordered pairs of child digests, and continue until one root remains. An authentication path supplies one sibling digest at each level; the index determines left versus right at every step.

For a balanced tree with leaves there are levels. If each digest has bits, an opening uses bits. The prover retains the proof and tree; the root by itself is not enough to generate an opening.

Computational binding prevents an efficient prover from changing the bit at an authenticated position after committing. It does not say the committed bits form a valid PCP proof. Verification must check that next.

Authentication and truth are different checks

The prover first fixes a PCP proof by sending its Merkle root. Only then does the verifier choose the random tests. The protocol must authenticate the answers and check what those answers say about the public claim.

For a false statement, the fixed proof passes each independently sampled PCP test with probability at most . Requiring every test to pass gives , plus the negligible probability of breaking the commitment’s binding guarantee. The result is a computational argument because the commitment is what enforces consistency in the real protocol.

Count the communication in bits

Let be statement length, PCP length, the constant number of queries per test, and the number of repetitions and digest length. Keeping these names separate prevents a short root from being confused with a short proof.

MessageBits sent
Rootλ
kλ query indicesO(λ log M)
kλ bits and pathsO(λ² log M)

Why does become ? If for a fixed constant , then . Thus total communication is . Polynomial growth in a logarithm is called polylogarithmic.

The verifier still reads the public input and runs the PCP’s query-selection and test algorithms. The HW3 theorem promises those algorithms are efficient; its communication calculation alone does not establish the stronger nearly linear verification time in the lecture’s SNARG definition.

HW3 4a · Build a succinct interactive argument

A PCP prover produces a bit string of length for a statement of length . A PCP verifier reads a constant number of positions chosen before seeing their bits, has perfect completeness and soundness error . A Merkle commitment has bits and position openings of bits. Construct a three-message argument with negligible soundness error and total communication .

Show step-by-step solution

  1. A PCP is a specially encoded proof whose randomly selected local tests detect false statements. It is not an ordinary witness with arbitrary bits sampled. Compute the PCP string, commit to all its indexed bits with a Merkle root , and send . Keep the string and tree so openings can be produced.

  2. The verifier independently chooses the random coins for PCP tests and sends all requested positions in one batch. Nonadaptive means the positions depend on the statement and coins, not on previously returned bits. The prover replies with each requested bit and its authentication path, all in a third message.

  3. Perform both checks: each opening must authenticate the returned bit at its requested position under , and each PCP test must accept when run on those bits. A valid Merkle path only proves “this bit was committed”; it does not prove the statement is true.

  4. For a true statement, honest PCP bits pass every local test and every opening verifies, giving perfect completeness. For a false statement, binding prevents the efficient prover from changing the committed proof after seeing queries. For a fixed proof, each independent PCP test accepts with probability at most . All tests pass with probability at most , plus a negligible term for breaking commitment binding.

  5. There are openings. Since is constant and , their total size is

    The root costs bits and indices cost , so they do not increase this bound. This proves the requested succinct communication; the stated PCP theorem alone does not promise a nearly linear verifier running time. The guarantee is an argument because Merkle binding assumes a computationally bounded attacker.

Hash the root to derive the tests

The PCP protocol’s middle message comes from public randomness. Once the statement and root are fixed, Fiat–Shamir can derive the verifier’s test randomness from . That randomness determines the requested positions and the local checks.

The root must be fixed before the random-oracle answer is known. Trying polynomially many roots costs polynomially many attempts against the amplified error. Distinct domain labels separate challenge hashing from the hashes that build the Merkle tree.

This establishes the homework’s succinct communication route. It does not supply zero knowledge, knowledge extraction or a faster PCP verifier by itself. Next we turn to polynomial oracles, which encode the structure of computations more directly.

HW3 4b · Remove the PCP challenge message

Convert the succinct argument in part 4(a) into a non-interactive argument in the random-oracle model.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. First compute the PCP string and its root . Then hash an unambiguous encoding of the public statement, root and protocol parameters. Use the random-oracle output to derive the independent verifier randomness for all PCP tests; those coins determine their query positions.

  2. The proof contains , the requested bits and their position openings. The verifier recomputes the challenge from the same context, authenticates the openings and runs every PCP local predicate. It accepts only if all checks pass.

  3. Fixing the root before hashing prevents tailoring the committed proof to a challenge already known. An attacker can try several roots, but the amplified per-attempt error is exponentially small; a polynomial number of attempts still gives negligible error in the intended random-oracle argument. The Merkle hash and challenge hash need distinct domain labels so the two roles are not confused.

  4. The proof stays short and is now one message: a succinct non-interactive argument, or SNARG, in the communication sense established in 4(a). Neither zero knowledge nor knowledge extraction was established by this construction. “Non-interactive” alone supplies neither property.

Arithmetic where division has a precise meaning

For the polynomial route, we work in a finite field for a prime number . Its elements are . Add and multiply normally, then keep the remainder modulo . For example, in , and .

The second equality says 5 is the multiplicative inverse of 3. Dividing by 3 therefore means multiplying by 5. Every nonzero field element has an inverse; zero does not. This is what allows cancellation: if and , multiplying by gives .

Primality is essential for this familiar remainder construction. Modulo 6, , so multiplying nonzero elements can give zero. Such elements are called zero divisors. Arithmetic modulo 6 is valid arithmetic, but it is not a field and cannot support every theorem we are about to use.

Field elements represent computation values in these proofs. Equality modulo is not automatically equality of unrestricted integers; integer claims need appropriate encoding and range constraints.

Read a polynomial as a rule with coefficients

A polynomial oracle promises more than a function that returns field values. It commits to one formal polynomial , with a fixed degree limit. Formal equality means equality of all coefficients; agreement at a few points is only evidence for that equality.

This distinction matters over finite fields. In , the nonzero formal polynomial evaluates to zero at all seven field elements. Its degree is large enough that the root bound permits this. We therefore need the degree to be small relative to the field if a random evaluation is to be informative.

The notation means polynomials whose coefficients lie in and whose degree is at most . The zero polynomial has all coefficients zero and is allowed even when the bound is zero. A prover cannot evade the limit by choosing a different high-degree polynomial after learning the evaluation point.

We will use that fixed-degree promise to connect a global identity to one local check. The next card proves the root bound that makes the connection work.

Why degree limits the number of roots

Over a field, a nonzero polynomial of degree has at most distinct roots. Here is the link between a root and the degree: if , polynomial division gives , with one degree smaller. The remainder is the constant , so it vanishes.

If a different value is also a root, then . Since has an inverse, . Thus every additional root belongs to the lower-degree polynomial . Repeating this argument uses one degree per distinct root; a nonzero constant has no roots.

The cancellation step explains exactly why “over a field” cannot be dropped. The next exercise tests that condition.

True or false: has at most two roots in . Here means arithmetic modulo 6, and a root is an input at which the polynomial evaluates to zero.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. The degree is 2, because the highest nonzero term is . The theorem “a nonzero degree- polynomial has at most roots” requires a field, where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.

  2. Modulo 6, even though neither factor is zero. Thus is not a field; we cannot cancel a nonzero factor as the root-bound proof requires.

  3. Evaluate all six inputs:

    The roots are . There are four of them, so the claim is false.

One random evaluation tests an identity

Suppose and each have degree at most . If they differ as formal polynomials, their difference is nonzero and has degree at most . They agree at exactly when .

Fix both polynomials first, then sample uniform . The root bound limits their agreement to at most field elements:

The denominator is the number of field elements. Choose a field much larger than the degree to make this error small. If the prover learned first, it could manufacture a different polynomial that agrees just there; the order of commitment and challenge is essential.

More variables: count total degree

The degree controlling a multivariate random check is the total degree. For example, consider this polynomial over :

The first term has total degree ; the second has total degree . The polynomial’s total degree is the maximum, 6. We count exponents within each term, then take the largest count.

The Schwartz–Zippel lemma extends the root test: for a nonzero formal polynomial of total degree , choose each input independently and uniformly from the same finite subset of a field. Then

The polynomial must be fixed before sampling the inputs. To test a proposed multivariable identity, subtract its two sides and apply this lemma to the difference. The rest of our PLONK outline uses univariate polynomials, meaning one input variable, but the same “false identity has few random zeros” idea underlies both tests.

Turn a table of values into one polynomial

For distinct field points and chosen values , there is exactly one polynomial of degree less than with . This is interpolation. It lets us encode a computation’s table of wire values as a polynomial.

To see existence, build a polynomial that is 1 at and 0 at every other table point:

The denominators are invertible because the points are distinct. At , only term remains, giving exactly . Each basis polynomial has degree . For uniqueness, two such interpolants would differ by a degree-below- polynomial with roots, contradicting the root bound.

Zero on a set is not zero everywhere

We often need only for a specified set of distinct points , read “Omega”. Define the vanishing polynomial

It has exactly the requested roots and degree . The factor argument from the root bound shows that vanishes at all points in exactly when divides . “Divides” means a polynomial exists with , with no remainder.

The quotient is a polynomial that certifies all those individual zero conditions at once. Next we will test its claimed factorization at a random point.

Check many zero conditions with one identity

Suppose the claim is that a degree-at-most- polynomial is zero at every point of a public set , with . We need to verify many equalities, but the factorization from the previous card expresses all of them as one identity:

The prover supplies a degree-bounded quotient oracle , fixed before the challenge. The verifier chooses uniform , queries and , computes , and accepts if . An honest factorization passes at every point, giving perfect completeness.

For a false claim, no permitted quotient makes the identity hold. Therefore is nonzero. Under the lecture’s loose bound , its degree is at most . The root bound gives soundness error at most .

The honest nonzero quotient needs degree only , but the looser oracle limit explains the lecture’s estimate. Verification multiplies rather than divides: it remains defined when , where . The verifier’s cost of evaluating this public polynomial must also be counted when assessing succinctness.

Encode an entire recurrence

Use the Fibonacci convention , with . Interpolate a degree-at-most-100 polynomial with for . The claim is that the last value is .

The verifier checks the endpoints , , . To check all recurrence steps, define

Require to vanish on . The prover fixes and a quotient ; after a random , the verifier checks

This uses seven polynomial evaluations: three endpoints, three shifted values at the random point, and one quotient value. The verifier derives from the same , so an unrelated “recurrence polynomial” cannot be substituted.

Work in a prime field with enough distinct points and, for this example’s integer interpretation, prime greater than . The recurrence fixes every value, all below that prime. The lecture writes initial values 1,1 but prints the answer for 0,1; this deck uses the consistent 0,1 convention. Also, few oracle queries alone do not make computing fast; we address that cost later.

Authenticate a polynomial evaluation

A polynomial commitment scheme (PCS) lets a prover bind itself to a polynomial and later authenticate an evaluation without sending all its coefficients. The lecture defines four algorithms:

AlgorithmIts input and output
Setup(d,λ) → ppGenerate public parameters for a degree limit and security parameter.
Commit(pp,f) → cPublish a commitment to f ∈ F[X]≤d.
Open(pp,f,r) → πProduce evidence for the claimed value y = f(r).
Verify(pp,c,r,y,π)Accept or reject that evaluation claim.

Correctness requires every honestly generated opening to verify:

where are generated by Setup, Commit and Open, for every allowed . The probability includes their random choices.

Evaluation binding says that every PPT has negligible probability of producing with

Both accepted claims concern the same commitment and evaluation point. The compiler must additionally justify treating the accepted answers as evaluations of one polynomial within the degree bound. The displayed evaluation-binding game alone is not that whole theorem. Hiding is also a separate property.

The order of commitments makes the test meaningful

We can now replace the ideal polynomial interfaces in ZeroTest with commitments. The algebra remains the same; what changes is how the verifier trusts the evaluation answers.

If the prover knew before fixing , it could often choose a constant just to satisfy the one displayed equation. The root-bound argument would then be invalid: the false polynomial would depend on the point at which it was tested.

Fiat–Shamir replaces the challenge message by a hash of the statement, public context and preceding commitments. A compiler theorem must account for the PCS guarantees, all challenge rounds and the random-oracle model. A three-message outline alone does not establish Sigma properties or zero knowledge.

A computation becomes a public relation

An arithmetic circuit is a network of addition and multiplication gates over a field. Wires carry field elements. Public inputs are known to the verifier; private inputs are the witness. Circuit satisfaction is usually written : the designated output must be zero.

Our running example over computes . For public and private , the intermediate results are and , giving output .

To state this as a zero-output relation with public target , use . In the trace diagrams we display the three-gate computation fragment and check its output equals ; adding the final subtraction gives the normalized zero-output circuit. We do not claim the displayed fragment itself outputs zero.

Write down what every gate claims happened

An execution trace lists the values on the circuit’s wires. Each gate has three slots: left input, right input and output. We also reserve slots for the original public and private inputs.

GateLeftRightOutput
0: multiply248
1: add437
2: multiply8756

There are slots, where counts gates and counts original inputs. For three gates and three inputs, . Use for this table size; its interpolating polynomial will have degree less than .

The two appearances of 4 in the gate table are copies of input , which also has an original-input slot. A dishonest table could put different values in those slots. Checking each gate’s arithmetic is therefore not enough: later we must also check that connected wires agree.

Choose distinct addresses with a useful pattern

We want distinct field points at which to store the trace. A primitive N-th root of unity has , with no smaller positive exponent giving 1. Its powers are therefore distinct.

In , has order 12. Its first twelve powers give the addresses for our twelve slots. Multiplying an address by advances one slot; after the last slot it wraps back to 1. This multiplicative pattern will let one formula refer to a gate’s three adjacent slots.

What makes a trace a correct computation?

A trace must meet four independent requirements. Public-input slots must equal the claimed inputs; the output slot must equal the public target; each gate must compute its operation; and every copy of a wire must agree.

The private input is allowed to change between candidate witnesses; the verifier does not know it. Its repeated appearances must still agree. The interactive alternatives each satisfy three requirements while violating exactly one, showing why none can simply be omitted.

Computing the public-input encoding may take time proportional to the number of public inputs. That is compatible with the verifier’s unavoidable cost of reading them.

Local arithmetic does not connect the gates

The wiring check can be encoded by a permutation of trace positions. For each physical wire, place all slots carrying that wire into one cycle. Call the resulting permutation . Requiring each value to equal the value at its successor forces all copies in a cycle to agree.

The private input’s two slots are included: privacy does not excuse inconsistent copies. Conceptually, form the polynomial whose domain values are the permuted trace and require equality on the domain. A real proof must also authenticate that permutation relationship; supplying an arbitrary second polynomial would not establish it.

A short formula removes a hidden linear cost

Querying only a few values is useful only if the verifier can also compute its own expressions quickly. Directly evaluating uses one factor per domain point.

Repeated squaring needs field multiplications. It is the structured domain that makes this fast; merely precomputing the coefficients of a degree- polynomial would still leave many evaluation operations.

The formula applies to the full root domain. Public-input and gate subsets need their own efficient formulas or authenticated preprocessed polynomials. In our twelve-slot example, the three gate addresses are only a subset; substituting for their vanishing polynomial would impose a different condition.

Assemble the argument and state its scope

The circuit-dependent work can be reused across many statements about the same circuit. Universal setup supports different circuits up to its degree limit; it does not mean every circuit needs no preprocessing.

The conceptual chain is now connected: interpolation encodes a trace; constraints say what makes it valid; quotient identities turn many constraints into a few random checks; polynomial commitments authenticate the answers; Fiat–Shamir removes verifier messages under the relevant security theorem.

The lecture sketches this route to PLONK. A complete implementation additionally specifies its permutation protocol, all challenge rounds, degree enforcement and security assumptions. Zero knowledge requires suitable blinding, meaning randomization that conceals witness information while preserving the checked constraints. Knowledge extraction requires a separate proof-of-knowledge argument. Neither follows just from short proofs.
